name: Rechta
desc: Algerian thin noodles steamed and served with chicken, chickpeas and turnips in a light, cinnamon-scented white sauce. A festive dish, especially around Algiers.
origin_note: Rechta is a traditional Algerian dish, strongly associated with Algiers and served at family celebrations and religious festivals. Fresh hand-rolled rechta noodles are ideal; thin dried noodles or fine tagliatelle are a practical substitute.
steps: Start the sauce|10|Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat and cook the onions 6 to 8 minutes until soft and translucent. Add the chicken, cinnamon stick, pepper and salt and turn the pieces for 3 to 4 minutes until lightly coloured.
Simmer|30|Add the water and chickpeas, bring to a boil, skim, then cover and simmer gently 30 minutes until the chicken is tender.
Add the turnips|20|Add the turnips and simmer 15 to 20 minutes until tender, and the chicken is cooked through (75 °C inside). The sauce should be light and savoury; adjust the salt.

Steam the noodles|20|Rub the noodles with a little oil, then steam them in a steamer or lined colander over the simmering pot for about 15 minutes until tender. Sprinkle with a few spoonfuls of broth and steam 5 minutes more.
Finish|3|Toss the hot noodles with the butter until glossy and separate. Pile on a platter, arrange the chicken and vegetables on top and ladle over the sauce.
tips: Steaming, not boiling, keeps rechta light and separate.
Serve extra sauce on the side so everyone can adjust.
mistakes: Boiling the noodles in the sauce makes them gummy.
storage: Refrigerate noodles and sauce separately up to 3 days.
reheat: Re-steam the noodles; heat the sauce until simmering (75 °C).
subs: noodles-thin>spaghetti|break into short lengths and cook until al dente

name: Mhadjeb
desc: Thin semolina flatbreads folded around a soft filling of slow-cooked tomato, onion and pepper, then cooked on a hot griddle until golden and crisp at the edges.
origin_note: Mhadjeb (also written mahdjouba or m’hajeb) is a popular Algerian street food and home snack, also found in Tunisia and Morocco under similar names. Fillings vary; tomato and pepper is the classic.
steps: Make the dough|10|Mix the semolina and salt, then add the water gradually, kneading 8 to 10 minutes until you have a smooth, firm, slightly elastic dough. Cover and rest 30 minutes.

Cook the filling|25|Heat the olive oil over medium heat, cook the onion 6 minutes until soft, add the garlic, pepper and spices for 1 minute, then the tomato and salt. Simmer 15 to 20 minutes, stirring, until thick and almost dry. Cool.

Shape|15|Divide the dough into 12 balls. Oil your work surface and roll or stretch each ball into a very thin square. Spoon filling onto the middle, fold the four sides in like an envelope and flatten gently into a square.
Cook|15|Heat a heavy griddle or non-stick pan over medium heat with a little oil. Cook each mhadjeb 3 to 4 minutes per side until golden brown and crisp in spots. Serve hot.
tips: Thin dough gives the crisp edges; oil the surface well to stretch it without tearing.
Cook the filling until dry, or the flatbreads turn soggy.
mistakes: A wet filling makes the dough tear.
reheat: Reheat in a dry pan until crisp and hot.

name: Makroud
desc: Diamond-shaped semolina pastries filled with spiced date paste, fried until golden and soaked in honey syrup. A classic sweet for Eid and celebrations.
origin_note: Makroud (maqrut) is a traditional sweet of Algeria and Tunisia, where it has regional styles (for example the Kairouan version in Tunisia); it can be fried or baked.
steps: Make the dough|15|Rub the semolina, melted butter and salt together with your fingertips until the grains look like damp sand and hold when squeezed. Add the orange blossom water and enough water to form a soft, non-sticky dough. Rest 1 hour covered.
Make the filling|5|Knead the dates with the cinnamon and 20 g butter into a smooth, pliable paste.

Shape|25|Roll the dough into a 1.5 cm thick rectangle, make a lengthwise groove, press a log of date paste in it, and close the dough over it. Flatten slightly to about 2 cm thick and cut into diamonds.
Fry|20|Heat the oil to about 170 °C. Fry in batches 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until deep golden. Drain on paper. Take care with hot oil.
Soak in syrup|10|Warm the honey with 100 ml water for 2 minutes. Drop the hot makroud into the warm syrup for 1 to 2 minutes, turn once, and lift out onto a rack. Cool before serving.
tips: The dough should feel like wet sand that holds together; too much water makes the pastry hard.
Drop hot pastry into warm (not boiling) syrup so it absorbs it without turning soggy.
mistakes: Oil that is too hot browns the outside before the dough cooks through.
storage: Airtight container at room temperature up to 1 week.
reheat: Serve at room temperature.
subs: honey>sugar|make a syrup of 250 g sugar and 150 ml water (suitable for vegans)

name: Bourek
desc: Crisp fried pastry cigars filled with spiced minced beef, onion and parsley. A staple of the Algerian Ramadan table.
origin_note: Bourek is a pastry found across the Ottoman-influenced Mediterranean; the minced-meat cigar form is a standard Algerian Ramadan dish (also eaten in Tunisia and elsewhere).
steps: Cook the filling|12|Heat 2 tbsp oil in a pan, cook the onion 5 minutes until soft, add the beef, paprika, pepper and salt and cook 6 to 8 minutes, breaking it up, until browned and no pink remains. Cool, then stir in the parsley and one beaten egg.
Fill|10|Place a halved filo sheet with the short side towards you, put 1 heaped tablespoon of filling near the edge, fold in the sides and roll up tightly like a cigar. Seal the end with beaten egg.
Heat the oil|4|Heat the frying oil to about 170 °C in a deep pan. Cover unused pastry with a damp cloth so it does not dry out.
Fry|10|Fry the boureks in batches for 2 to 3 minutes, turning, until golden and crisp. Drain on paper towel. Serve hot with lemon.
tips: Cool the filling fully before rolling or the pastry tears.
Bake at 200 °C for 15 to 20 minutes, brushed with oil, for a lighter version.
mistakes: Rolling loosely lets oil in and makes them greasy.
storage: Refrigerate cooked up to 2 days; freeze uncooked.
reheat: Crisp in a 190 °C oven for 8 minutes until hot throughout.
subs: beef-mince>potato-boiled|vegetarian filling with the same spices

name: Tabbouleh
desc: A bright Levantine salad that is mostly parsley, with finely diced tomato, mint, spring onion and a little bulgur, dressed with lemon and olive oil.
origin_note: Tabbouleh is a staple of Lebanese and Syrian cuisine and listed here for both; the Lebanese version is herb-heavy with little bulgur. Versions with more grain (including the French taboulé) are far from the original proportions.
ing: 3 bunch|parsley|flat-leaf, leaves only, very finely chopped
steps: Soak the bulgur|15|Rinse the bulgur, cover with the diced tomato juices and 2 tbsp of the lemon juice and leave 15 minutes until tender but with some bite.
Prepare the herbs|15|Wash and dry the parsley and mint thoroughly, then chop very finely with a sharp knife, working in small bunches so the leaves are cut rather than bruised.
Combine|3|Mix the herbs, tomato, spring onion and bulgur in a large bowl.
Dress|2|Add the remaining lemon juice, olive oil, salt and allspice and toss gently. Taste and adjust the lemon and salt. Serve right away, ideally with crisp lettuce or cabbage leaves for scooping.
tips: Dry the herbs well so the salad is not watery.
Dress just before serving so the parsley stays bright.
mistakes: Too much bulgur turns it into a grain salad rather than a herb salad.
storage: Best the same day; keeps 1 day refrigerated.
reheat: Serve cold.
subs: bulgur>rice-white|gluten-free alternative; cook and cool it first

name: Fattoush
desc: A crunchy Levantine salad of cucumber, tomato, lettuce and herbs topped with crisp fried or toasted flatbread and a tangy sumac and lemon dressing.
origin_note: Fattoush is a staple across Lebanon and Syria and is eaten widely in the Levant. It is a bread salad created to use up stale flatbread.
steps: Toast the bread|8|Toss the torn flatbread with 3 tbsp oil and bake at 200 °C for 6 to 8 minutes, turning once, until golden and crisp. Cool completely.
Make the dressing|3|Whisk together the lemon juice, 4 tbsp oil, garlic, 1 tsp sumac and salt until emulsified.
Combine the vegetables|7|In a large bowl mix the lettuce, tomato, cucumber, spring onion, parsley and mint.
Finish|2|Just before serving, pour over the dressing, toss gently, add the toasted bread and sprinkle with the remaining sumac.
tips: Add the bread at the last moment to keep it crunchy.
Sumac gives the characteristic lemony tang.
mistakes: Dressing too early makes everything soggy.
storage: Best fresh; vegetables keep 1 day, store bread separately.
reheat: Serve cold.
subs: sumac>lemon-juice|add 1 extra tbsp lemon juice and a little zest

name: Baba ghanoush
desc: A smoky dip of roasted aubergine blended with tahini, lemon and garlic, served with olive oil and warm bread.
origin_note: Baba ghanoush is a Levantine dip associated with Lebanon, Syria and neighbouring countries; the name and exact recipe vary. Mutabbal is a closely related, tahini-rich version.
steps: Roast the aubergines|45|Prick the aubergines, then roast them whole at 220 °C for 40 to 45 minutes, turning once, until the skins blacken and the flesh collapses. For extra smokiness char them over a gas flame first.
Drain|10|Slit them open and scoop the flesh into a colander. Leave 10 minutes to drain bitter juices, pressing gently.
Mix|4|Chop or mash the flesh coarsely and mix with the tahini, lemon juice, garlic, salt and cumin until creamy but still slightly chunky.
Serve|1|Spoon into a shallow dish, drizzle with olive oil and sprinkle with parsley. Serve with warm bread.
tips: The skin should be completely blackened; undercooked aubergine tastes bitter.
Mash by hand for texture.
mistakes: Skipping the draining makes the dip watery.
reheat: Serve cold or at room temperature.

name: Mujaddara
desc: Humble, deeply savoury lentils and rice topped with a heap of slowly caramelised onions, a staple of Levantine home cooking.
origin_note: Mujaddara is eaten across Lebanon, Syria, Palestine and Jordan and the wider Arab world with local variations (some versions use bulgur). Its exact origin is not agreed.
steps: Caramelise the onions|35|Heat the olive oil in a wide pan over medium-low heat. Cook the onions for 30 to 35 minutes, stirring often, until deep golden brown and crisp at the edges. Remove half for topping.
Cook the lentils|20|Add the lentils and water to the pan with the remaining onions, bring to a boil, then simmer 20 minutes until the lentils are nearly tender.
Add the rice|20|Stir in the rice, cumin, salt and pepper, cover and cook over low heat 15 to 20 minutes until the rice and lentils are soft and all liquid is absorbed.
Serve|2|Rest 5 minutes, fluff gently, top with the reserved onions and serve with yoghurt or a simple salad.
tips: Patience with the onions is the whole dish; low heat prevents bitterness.
Stir only occasionally so the grains stay whole.
mistakes: Rushing the onions over high heat makes them bitter.
reheat: Reheat with a splash of water.

name: Menemen
desc: Soft, creamy eggs scrambled with tomatoes and green peppers, a Turkish breakfast served in the pan with bread.
origin_note: Menemen is a classic Turkish breakfast dish, named after a town in İzmir province; there is a well-known friendly debate about whether to add onion.
steps: Soften the vegetables|8|Melt the butter in a wide pan over medium heat and cook the peppers and onion 6 to 8 minutes until soft.
Cook the tomatoes|6|Add the tomatoes and salt and cook 5 to 6 minutes, stirring, until the juices reduce to a thick sauce.
Add the eggs|4|Make a few gaps in the sauce and crack in the eggs. Stir gently with a fork, cooking 2 to 3 minutes until just set but still soft and creamy; eggs should not be raw.
Serve|1|Sprinkle with chilli flakes and bring the pan straight to the table with plenty of bread.
tips: Remove from the heat while still slightly glossy; the eggs continue to cook.
Peeling the tomatoes gives a smoother result.
mistakes: Overcooking turns the eggs dry and grainy.
reheat: Not recommended.

name: Lentil soup
desc: A silky red lentil soup with onion, carrot and cumin, finished with lemon. Everyday comfort food, especially in Ramadan.
origin_note: Red lentil soup (shorbat adas) is a staple in Egypt and across the Levant and the Arab world; recipes differ slightly by country, and it is also common in Turkey.
steps: Soften the vegetables|8|Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat, cook the onion and carrot 6 to 8 minutes until soft, then add the garlic and cumin for 1 minute.
Cook the lentils|25|Add the lentils, water and salt, bring to a boil and skim any foam. Simmer partly covered 20 to 25 minutes until the lentils are completely soft.
Blend|3|Blend the soup with a stick blender until smooth and creamy, adding a little hot water if it is too thick.
Finish|1|Stir in the lemon juice, taste for salt and serve hot with lemon wedges and bread.
tips: Red lentils need no soaking.
A pinch of ground cumin on top adds aroma.
mistakes: Adding lemon during cooking dulls the flavour.
storage: Refrigerate up to 4 days; freezes well.
reheat: Reheat with water until steaming.

name: Chana masala
desc: Chickpeas simmered in a tangy, spiced tomato and onion gravy, a North Indian and Pakistani staple eaten with rice, roti or bhatura.
origin_note: Chana masala is a staple of Punjabi cooking and eaten across India and Pakistan; the chickpea-and-tomato combination appears in many regional forms.
steps: Brown the onions|10|Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and cook the onions 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until golden brown.
Add the paste and spices|3|Stir in the ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then the cumin, coriander, turmeric and chilli powder for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Cook the gravy|10|Add the tomatoes and salt and cook 8 to 10 minutes until the oil begins to separate at the edges of the sauce.
Simmer the chickpeas|12|Add the chickpeas and water, simmer 10 to 12 minutes, mashing a few chickpeas against the pan to thicken. Stir in the garam masala and lemon juice.
Serve|1|Scatter with fresh coriander and serve with rice or flatbread.
tips: Cook the tomatoes until the oil separates for a rounder flavour.
Add the garam masala at the end to keep its aroma.
mistakes: Rushing the onions gives a raw, harsh taste.
storage: Refrigerate up to 4 days; freezes well.
reheat: Reheat with a splash of water.
subs: chickpeas-cooked>chickpeas-dried|soak overnight and boil 1 hour first

name: Palak paneer
desc: Cubes of soft paneer cheese in a velvety spinach gravy with onion, tomato and warm spices.
origin_note: Palak paneer is a North Indian vegetarian dish, especially associated with Punjab, and a menu staple across India and the Indian diaspora.
steps: Blanch the spinach|4|Boil the spinach in a large pot for 1 to 2 minutes until wilted, then drain, cool in cold water and squeeze dry. Blend to a coarse puree.
Start the base|10|Heat the ghee in a pan over medium heat, add the cumin seeds until they sizzle, then the onion 6 minutes until golden. Add the ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute.
Cook the tomatoes|8|Add the tomatoes, turmeric and salt and cook 6 to 8 minutes until soft and broken down.
Add spinach and paneer|7|Stir in the spinach puree and 100 ml water and simmer 5 minutes. Add the paneer and cream and warm through 3 minutes without boiling hard. Add the garam masala.
Serve|2|Spoon into a warm dish, add a swirl of cream if you like, and serve hot with roti, naan or steamed basmati rice.
tips: Cooling the spinach in cold water keeps its colour bright.
Soak fried paneer in warm water for softer cubes.
mistakes: Overcooking the spinach turns it dull and bitter.
reheat: Reheat gently; do not boil hard.
subs: paneer>tofu-firm|vegan; also swap cream for coconut-milk and ghee for oil

name: Aloo gobi
desc: A dry-style curry of potato and cauliflower with cumin, turmeric and ginger, cooked until tender with lightly browned edges.
origin_note: Aloo gobi is a popular vegetarian dish across India and Pakistan, with many regional variations in spicing and moisture.
steps: Temper the spices|3|Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds until they sizzle, then the onion, ginger and chilli and cook 5 to 6 minutes until the onion is soft.
Add the potatoes|10|Add the potatoes, turmeric, coriander and salt, stir, cover and cook 8 to 10 minutes, stirring now and then.

Add cauliflower and tomato|15|Add the cauliflower and tomatoes, cover and cook 12 to 15 minutes over medium-low heat, stirring gently, until both vegetables are tender when pierced but still hold their shape. Add a splash of water if sticking.
Finish|2|Uncover and cook 2 minutes to dry the pan slightly. Scatter with coriander and serve with roti.
tips: Do not add much water; the vegetables steam in their own moisture.
Stir gently to avoid mashing the cauliflower.
mistakes: Too much liquid makes a stew rather than a dry curry.
reheat: Reheat in a pan until steaming.

name: Chicken tikka masala
desc: Yoghurt-marinated chicken chunks, grilled until charred and simmered in a spiced, creamy tomato sauce.
origin_note: The origin of chicken tikka masala is disputed: it is widely associated with South Asian cooks in Britain (often Glasgow is cited), while others trace it to Punjab-style tandoori dishes in India or Pakistan. Both countries are listed.
steps: Marinate|120|Mix the chicken with the yoghurt, lemon juice, half the ginger-garlic paste, 1 tsp garam masala, the chilli powder and half the salt. Marinate at least 2 hours, or overnight, in the fridge.
Grill the chicken|12|Cook the chicken on a very hot grill pan or under a hot grill 10 to 12 minutes, turning, until charred in spots and cooked through (75 °C inside).

Make the sauce|20|Heat the oil, cook the onion 8 minutes until golden, add the remaining paste, cumin and paprika for 1 minute, then the tomatoes and remaining salt. Simmer 12 minutes and blend until smooth if you like.
Combine|8|Add the chicken and cream, simmer 6 to 8 minutes without boiling hard, then stir in the remaining garam masala. Top with coriander and serve with rice or naan.
tips: Charring the chicken gives the typical smoky flavour.
Do not marinate longer than 24 hours or the chicken turns mushy.
mistakes: Boiling the sauce after adding cream can split it.
reheat: Reheat gently until steaming hot (75 °C).

name: Kimchi jjigae
desc: A bubbling Korean stew of well-fermented kimchi, pork belly and tofu, tangy, spicy and deeply comforting.
origin_note: Kimchi jjigae is among the most common everyday stews in Korea, traditionally made with aged, sour kimchi. Kimjang, the making and sharing of kimchi, is on UNESCO’s intangible heritage list (South Korea 2013, and North Korea 2015); this stew is a home-cooking staple rather than a ritual dish.
steps: Fry the pork|6|Heat the sesame oil in a pot over medium heat and fry the pork belly 5 to 6 minutes until the fat is rendered and the meat is lightly browned.
Add the kimchi|6|Add the kimchi, onion and garlic and stir-fry 5 minutes until the kimchi softens and smells sweetly sour.
Simmer|18|Add the chilli flakes and water, bring to a boil, then simmer 15 to 18 minutes until the pork is tender and cooked through.
Add the tofu|5|Add the tofu and simmer 4 to 5 minutes more. Taste and add a little salt if needed, then top with spring onion and serve bubbling with rice.
tips: Older, sour kimchi gives a much better stew.
Add a splash of kimchi juice for extra tang.
mistakes: Using fresh, mild kimchi gives a flat flavour.
reheat: Reheat until bubbling.
subs: pork-belly>mushroom|vegetarian, add 1 tsp soy sauce; most kimchi still contains fish sauce

name: Onigiri
desc: Japanese rice balls shaped by hand around a savoury filling and wrapped in crisp nori, a lunchbox and convenience-store favourite.
origin_note: Onigiri is a traditional Japanese food with centuries of history as portable rice. Common fillings include umeboshi, salmon and tuna with mayonnaise.
steps: Cook the rice|25|Rinse the rice until the water runs nearly clear, then cook with the 400 ml water, covered, over low heat 15 minutes after it comes to a boil, and rest 10 minutes. Fluff and let cool until warm enough to handle.
Make the filling|3|Mix the tuna with the mayonnaise until creamy.

Shape|12|Wet your hands and rub them with a little salt. Take about 100 g of warm rice, press a hollow in the middle, add a spoonful of filling, close the rice around it and shape into a triangle with firm but gentle pressure.
Wrap|3|Wrap each onigiri with a strip of nori just before eating so it stays crisp, and sprinkle with sesame seeds.
tips: Use warm rice; cold rice will not stick together.
Do not squeeze too hard: the rice should stay light.
mistakes: Using long-grain rice; it does not hold its shape.
storage: Eat within a few hours, or refrigerate wrapped up to 1 day (the rice firms up).
reheat: Warm briefly in a microwave for 15 seconds if desired.
subs: tuna-canned>tofu|vegetarian, with a pinch of salt and sesame

name: Prawn and vegetable tempura
desc: Prawns and vegetables in an ice-cold, lightly mixed batter, fried until pale, light and crisp, with a soy dipping sauce.
origin_note: Tempura is a Japanese dish, though its frying technique is commonly said to have been introduced by Portuguese traders in the 16th century.
steps: Prepare the sauce|2|Mix the soy sauce, mirin and the 3 tbsp water for dipping.
Prepare the ingredients|10|Make 3 shallow cuts on the underside of each prawn and straighten it so it does not curl. Pat the prawns and vegetables dry and dust with a little flour.
Make the batter|3|Beat the egg with the ice-cold water, then stir in the flour and cornstarch with chopsticks for only a few seconds; the batter should be lumpy.
Heat the oil|5|Heat the oil in a deep pan to 170 to 180 °C; a drop of batter should sink slightly then rise and sizzle.

Fry|12|Dip each piece in batter and fry in small batches, 2 to 3 minutes for vegetables and 2 minutes for prawns, until pale golden and crisp. Drain on a rack and serve immediately with the dipping sauce.
tips: Keep the batter cold and barely mixed for a lacy, crisp coating.
Fry in small batches to keep the oil temperature steady.
mistakes: Overmixing the batter makes the tempura heavy and chewy.
reheat: Re-crisp in a 200 °C oven for 5 minutes (not as good).

name: Egg fried rice
desc: Fluffy rice stir-fried with scrambled egg, peas and spring onion in a hot wok, seasoned simply with soy and a touch of sesame.
origin_note: Egg fried rice is a classic of Chinese home cooking and the base of many regional fried-rice dishes; Yangzhou fried rice is the famous variant.
steps: Scramble the eggs|3|Heat 1 tbsp oil in a wok over high heat. Pour in the eggs and stir 30 to 40 seconds until just set, then remove.
Fry the aromatics|2|Add the remaining oil and stir-fry the white parts of the spring onion and the peas for 1 minute.
Fry the rice|4|Add the cold rice, pressing to break up clumps, and stir-fry 3 to 4 minutes over high heat until hot and the grains jump separately in the pan.
Season|2|Return the eggs, add the soy sauce, salt and pepper and toss for 1 minute. Finish with sesame oil and the green parts of the spring onion.
tips: Cold, day-old rice is the secret; cool leftover rice quickly and refrigerate within an hour.
Keep the heat high and the wok moving.
mistakes: Fresh warm rice turns mushy in the wok.
storage: Eat promptly; refrigerate within 1 hour and use within 1 day.
reheat: Reheat until steaming hot throughout.

name: Shepherd’s pie
desc: A rich lamb mince and vegetable filling in gravy, topped with creamy mashed potato and baked until golden.
origin_note: Shepherd’s pie is a British and Irish dish dating from the late 18th century, traditionally made with lamb (cottage pie uses beef).
steps: Boil the potatoes|20|Boil the potatoes in salted water 15 to 20 minutes until tender, drain and mash with the butter, milk and a pinch of salt until smooth.
Cook the mince|12|Heat the oil, cook the onion and carrot 6 minutes, add the lamb and brown 6 minutes, breaking it up, until no pink remains.
Make the gravy|15|Stir in the tomato paste, Worcestershire sauce, stock, thyme and salt, then simmer uncovered 12 to 15 minutes until thick. Add the peas for the last 3 minutes.
Assemble and bake|30|Heat the oven to 200 °C. Spoon the filling into a baking dish, top with the mash and rough it up with a fork. Bake 25 to 30 minutes until golden and bubbling at the edges.
Rest|10|Rest the pie for 10 minutes after baking so the filling settles and slices hold together, then serve with greens.
tips: A fork-roughened top browns more.
Let the filling thicken well so it does not seep through the mash.
mistakes: Watery filling makes the potato sink.
storage: Refrigerate up to 3 days; freezes well.
reheat: Reheat covered at 180 °C until hot all the way through.

name: Fish and chips
desc: Crisp beer-battered white fish with thick golden chips, salt and vinegar, the classic British takeaway.
origin_note: Fish and chips became a British working-class staple in the 19th century; fried fish was introduced by Jewish immigrants and chips were added in northern England. Exact first shops are disputed.
steps: Soak the chips|10|Rinse the chips in cold water to remove starch, then dry thoroughly with a cloth.
First fry|10|Heat the oil to 150 °C and fry the chips in batches for 6 to 8 minutes until soft but not coloured. Drain.
Make the batter|3|Whisk the flour, baking powder and salt with the cold beer into a smooth, thick batter. Pat the fish dry and dust with flour.
Fry the fish|8|Heat the oil to 180 °C. Dip each fillet in batter and fry 5 to 6 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and the fish is opaque and flakes easily.
Finish the chips|4|Fry the chips again at 180 °C for 3 to 4 minutes until golden and crisp. Salt well and serve with the fish, vinegar and lemon.
tips: Dry the fish and dust it with flour so the batter sticks.
Keep the oil temperature steady by frying in small batches.
mistakes: Cold, wet chips lower the oil temperature and turn greasy.
reheat: Re-crisp in a 200 °C oven for 8 minutes.
subs: beer>water|sparkling water gives a similar light batter and no alcohol

name: Tortilla española
desc: A thick Spanish omelette of tender, slowly cooked potato and onion held together with egg, served warm or at room temperature.
origin_note: Tortilla de patatas is a national staple of Spain; its exact origin is unclear and the debate over whether to include onion is famous.
steps: Poach the potatoes|20|Heat the oil in a 24 cm non-stick pan over medium-low heat. Add the potatoes and onion with half the salt and cook 15 to 20 minutes, turning often, until completely tender but not browned.
Mix|5|Drain the potatoes, reserving the oil. Beat the eggs with the remaining salt in a large bowl, fold in the warm potatoes and rest 5 minutes.
Cook the first side|6|Heat 1 tbsp of the reserved oil in the pan over medium heat, pour in the mixture and cook 5 to 6 minutes until the base is golden and the edges set, shaking the pan.
Flip|5|Place a large plate on top, flip the pan, slide the tortilla back in and cook the second side 3 to 4 minutes until set but still slightly soft in the centre; eggs should not be raw.
Rest|10|Rest at least 10 minutes before cutting.
tips: Cook the potatoes gently in oil, not fry hard.
The centre can stay soft, but not liquid.
mistakes: Browning the potatoes makes the tortilla dry.
reheat: Serve at room temperature or warm gently.

name: Greek salad
desc: Ripe tomatoes, cucumber, red onion, olives and a slab of feta with oregano and generous olive oil, no lettuce.
origin_note: Horiatiki (village salad) is the traditional Greek summer salad; its modern form with tomatoes and cucumber became popular in the 20th century.
steps: Prepare the vegetables|10|Cut the tomatoes into wedges, slice the cucumber and onion, and place in a wide bowl with the olives.
Season|2|Sprinkle with the salt and toss gently; the tomatoes will release juices that become the dressing.
Add the feta|2|Place the whole slab of feta on top and sprinkle with the oregano.
Dress and rest|10|Drizzle with the olive oil and vinegar and leave 10 minutes at room temperature before serving with crusty bread to mop up the juices.
tips: Use the ripest tomatoes you can find; the salad depends on them.
Serve at room temperature.
mistakes: Adding lettuce changes the traditional salad.
reheat: Serve cold or at room temperature.
subs: feta>tofu-firm|vegan; marinate in lemon and salt

name: Pizza margherita
desc: A thin, chewy pizza base with a bright tomato sauce, melting mozzarella and fresh basil, baked very hot.
origin_note: Pizza is associated with Naples, Italy. A popular story says the Margherita was created in 1889 to honour Queen Margherita of Savoy, but historians question that account, so treat it as legend.
steps: Make the dough|15|Mix the flour, yeast and salt, add the water and knead 10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
Prove|90|Cover and leave in a warm place 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled in size.
Prepare the oven and sauce|5|Heat the oven with a baking sheet or stone inside to its highest setting (240 to 250 °C). Mix the tomatoes with 1 tbsp oil and a pinch of salt.
Shape|10|Divide the dough into 4, stretch each by hand into a 25 cm round, spread with sauce and add mozzarella.
Bake|10|Slide the pizza onto the hot sheet and bake 8 to 10 minutes until the crust is puffed and charred in spots and the cheese is bubbling. Top with basil and the remaining oil.
tips: The hotter the oven, the better the crust.
Drain the mozzarella well so the pizza does not go soggy.
mistakes: Too much sauce or cheese makes the centre wet.
storage: Best fresh; leftovers keep 2 days refrigerated.
reheat: Reheat in a hot oven or pan, not a microwave.

name: Bœuf bourguignon
desc: Beef braised slowly in red wine with bacon, mushrooms and onions until meltingly tender, a classic of Burgundy.
origin_note: A traditional dish of Burgundy, France; it entered classic French cooking through 19th- and 20th-century restaurant cuisine.
steps: Brown the meat|20|Pat the beef dry and brown in batches in a casserole in the oil, 3 to 4 minutes per batch. Remove, then fry the bacon 4 minutes until crisp.
Cook the vegetables|10|Add the onions and carrots to the fat and cook 6 to 8 minutes. Stir in the garlic, flour and tomato paste for 1 minute.
Add the liquid|5|Return the beef and bacon, pour in the wine and stock, add the thyme, bay leaves and salt and bring to a simmer, scraping up the browned bits.
Braise|150|Cover and cook in a 160 °C oven for 2 to 2.5 hours until the beef is very tender and the sauce has thickened.
Finish|10|Fry the mushrooms in the butter 5 to 6 minutes until golden and stir into the stew. Discard the thyme stems and bay leaves; serve with potatoes or bread.
tips: Dry the meat well for a proper brown crust.
Better made a day ahead.
mistakes: Overcrowding the pan steams the meat instead of browning it.
storage: Refrigerate up to 4 days; freezes well.
reheat: Reheat gently on the hob until steaming.
subs: red-wine>beef-stock|alcohol-free; add 1 tbsp vinegar for acidity

name: Guacamole
desc: Creamy mashed avocado with lime, onion, coriander and chilli, served with tortilla chips or tacos.
origin_note: Guacamole comes from Mexico; its name derives from the Nahuatl ahuacamolli, meaning avocado sauce.
steps: Mash the avocado|3|Halve and stone the avocados, scoop the flesh into a bowl and mash roughly with a fork, leaving some chunks.
Add flavourings|3|Stir in the lime juice, onion, chilli, coriander and salt.
Fold in the tomato|1|Gently fold in the deseeded, diced tomato so the guacamole stays creamy with some chunks and the tomato does not turn watery.
Taste and serve|1|Adjust the lime and salt and serve immediately, since avocado browns quickly.
tips: Use ripe avocados that give slightly to gentle pressure.
Press cling film on the surface to slow browning.
mistakes: Over-mashing makes it a paste.
storage: Best fresh; refrigerate up to 1 day with plastic pressed on the surface.
reheat: Serve cold.

name: Arepas
desc: Griddled maize-flour patties with a crisp crust and soft centre, split and filled with cheese, a staple of Colombia and Venezuela.
origin_note: Arepas are a staple in both Colombia and Venezuela, each with its own styles and fillings, and with pre-Columbian roots in Indigenous maize cooking. Neither country is credited as the sole origin.
ing: 2 tbsp|butter|melted, plus extra for the pan
steps: Make the dough|5|Mix the water and salt, gradually add the maize flour while stirring, then knead in the melted butter. Rest 5 minutes; the dough should be soft and not sticky.
Shape|5|Form 8 balls and flatten each into a 10 cm disc about 1.5 cm thick, smoothing the cracks at the edges.
Cook|16|Cook on a lightly buttered griddle over medium heat 6 to 8 minutes per side until golden with a crisp crust and hollow-sounding when tapped.
Fill|2|Split each arepa open and fill with cheese; the heat will melt it. Serve warm.
tips: Wet your hands to smooth the edges.
Finish in a 180 °C oven for 10 minutes if the centre is doughy.
mistakes: A dry dough cracks at the edges; add a spoonful of warm water.
reheat: Toast in a pan or toaster.

name: Lomo saltado
desc: Peruvian stir-fry of beef strips, onion and tomato flamed with soy sauce and vinegar, served over rice with fries.
origin_note: Lomo saltado is a classic of chifa, the Chinese-Peruvian cuisine that grew from Chinese immigration to Peru in the 19th century, combining wok technique with Peruvian ingredients.
steps: Prepare the fries and rice|5|Fry the potato fries, or bake them at 220 °C for 30 minutes, until golden and cook the rice; keep both warm.
Marinate the beef|10|Toss the beef with 1 tbsp soy sauce, the garlic and a pinch of salt for 10 minutes.
Sear the beef|5|Heat 2 tbsp oil in a wok or large pan over very high heat. Sear the beef in two batches for 1 to 2 minutes each, until browned but still tender, then remove.
Stir-fry the vegetables|4|Add the onion, tomato and chilli to the hot pan for 2 minutes until just softened but still crisp.
Combine|2|Return the beef, add the remaining soy sauce and the vinegar, toss 1 minute and fold in the fries and coriander. Serve over rice at once.
tips: Very high heat and small batches create the smoky wok flavour.
Add the fries last so they stay somewhat crisp.
mistakes: Crowding the pan steams the beef.
reheat: Reheat in a hot pan.

name: Chimichurri
desc: A tangy, garlicky parsley and oregano sauce with olive oil and vinegar, the classic partner for Argentine grilled meat.
origin_note: Chimichurri is the signature sauce of Argentine asado and is also used in Uruguay and neighbouring countries; stories about the name are folk etymologies and unproven.
steps: Chop the herbs|10|Pick the parsley leaves, dry them and chop very finely by hand with a sharp knife for the best texture.
Combine|3|Mix the parsley, garlic, oregano and chilli flakes in a bowl and stir in the salt and vinegar.
Add oil|2|Stir in the olive oil until the sauce is loose and glossy.
Rest|30|Leave at room temperature for 30 minutes so the flavours blend. Serve with grilled steak, sausages or vegetables.
tips: Chop by hand; a blender makes a paste.
It improves after a few hours.
mistakes: Adding all the vinegar first can taste too sharp; taste as you go.
reheat: Bring to room temperature.

name: Ropa vieja
desc: Tender shredded beef stewed in a savoury tomato, pepper and olive sauce, the national dish of Cuba.
origin_note: Ropa vieja is regarded as a national dish of Cuba, with Spanish (Canary Islands) roots; its name means old clothes, for the shredded meat. Related dishes exist across the Spanish-speaking world.
steps: Simmer the beef|90|Put the beef, the quartered onion, bay leaves, half the garlic, the salt and the water in a pot, bring to a boil, skim, then simmer 1.5 hours until very tender.
Shred|10|Lift out the beef, shred it with two forks and keep 250 ml of the broth.
Make the sauce|15|Heat the oil, cook the sliced onion and peppers 8 minutes until soft, add the remaining garlic, cumin and oregano, then the tomato paste and crushed tomatoes and simmer 8 minutes.

Combine|25|Add the shredded beef, reserved broth, olives and vinegar and simmer 20 to 25 minutes until the sauce is thick and clings to the meat. Taste and adjust the salt. Serve with rice and black beans.
tips: Keep the cooking broth for soups.
Shred across the grain for tender strands.
mistakes: Cooking at a hard boil toughens the meat.
storage: Refrigerate up to 4 days; freezes well.
reheat: Reheat until steaming.

name: Macaroni and cheese
desc: Macaroni in a velvety cheddar sauce made from a roux, a comfort-food staple of American home cooking.
origin_note: Pasta with cheese dishes have European roots; macaroni and cheese became an American staple in the 18th to 20th centuries, popularised partly through cookbooks and later boxed versions.
steps: Cook the pasta|10|Boil the macaroni in salted water 1 minute less than the packet says, so it is just short of tender, then drain.
Make the roux|3|Melt the butter in a large pan over medium heat, whisk in the flour and cook 1 to 2 minutes, stirring, without browning.
Add the milk|8|Add the warm milk gradually, whisking constantly, and cook 6 to 8 minutes until the sauce is smooth and coats the back of a spoon.
Melt the cheese|3|Take off the heat and stir in the cheddar, salt and pepper until melted and smooth.
Combine|2|Fold in the pasta and serve at once, or bake with a crumb topping at 200 °C for 15 minutes.
tips: Warm milk and low heat keep the sauce smooth.
Add cheese off the heat so it does not turn grainy.
mistakes: Overcooking the pasta; it keeps cooking in the sauce.
reheat: Reheat with a splash of milk over low heat.

name: Fried plantain (dodo)
desc: Ripe plantain slices fried until caramelised and golden outside and soft inside, a sweet-savoury side or snack in Nigeria and across West Africa.
origin_note: Fried plantain (called dodo in Nigeria, aloko in Côte d’Ivoire, kelewele when spiced in Ghana) is eaten across West and Central Africa and the Caribbean.
steps: Prepare the plantains|5|Trim the ends, slit the skin lengthways and peel. Slice diagonally into 1 cm thick pieces.
Heat the oil|3|Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat until a slice sizzles gently when added; the oil should be about 170 °C.
Fry|8|Fry the slices in batches 2 to 3 minutes per side until deep golden brown and caramelised at the edges. Do not crowd the pan.
Drain|1|Lift out onto paper towel, sprinkle with a pinch of salt and serve hot.
tips: The riper the plantain, the sweeter and more caramelised.
Medium heat prevents burning the sugars before the inside softens.
mistakes: Using unripe green plantain gives a starchy, dry result.
reheat: Re-crisp in a hot pan or oven.

name: Chapati
desc: Soft, layered unleavened flatbread rolled with oil and cooked on a hot pan, a staple of East African and South Asian tables.
origin_note: Chapati came to East Africa with South Asian migrants and became a staple in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda, where the layered, oil-rolled version is typical. The flatbread itself originates in South Asia.
steps: Make the dough|10|Mix the flour, salt and sugar, add 2 tbsp oil and the warm water gradually, and knead 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and soft. Rest 30 minutes covered.
Layer|10|Divide into 8 balls. Roll one thin, brush with oil, roll up into a rope, coil it into a snail and flatten. Repeat, then rest 10 minutes.
Roll|5|Roll each coil out with a rolling pin into a round about 20 cm across and 2 mm thick, dusting lightly with flour so it does not stick.

Cook|15|Cook on a hot dry pan over medium heat 1 to 2 minutes, flip, brush with a little oil, cook 1 to 2 minutes more and flip again until golden with brown spots. Stack wrapped in a cloth to stay soft.
tips: The coiling step creates the soft layers.
Keep the cooked chapatis wrapped so they stay soft.
mistakes: A pan that is too cool dries the bread.
reheat: Warm in a dry pan for 30 seconds.
